title: Eleven Rigs Asleep
passages:
Miko rode the running board with her boots hooked over the frame and the wind packing dust down her collar. She had no name. Brill had rubbed her inked name off the storeroom steel, and her badge—C9-047—sat on a dead-name manifest clipped to Culvert Nine's board. She was cargo now, or something closer to it: a body without a plate, riding north on a rig that belonged to a man who kept names in a book.

Dray slowed the rig at the edge of Marrow Cut. The yard's door plate stood in the dirt—a slab of steel bolted to two posts, stamped with the yard's number and a line of rules Miko couldn't read from the running board. Dray cut the engine. The rig settled. The only sound was the tick of cooling metal and the wind down the spur.

"Out," Dray said.

Miko dropped to the ground. Her knees took the weight. Dray didn't offer a hand. He walked her to a scale bolted beside the door plate: a cast-iron platform with a dial face and a sliding weight. He gestured at it with his chin.

"Step on."

"I'm not freight," Miko said.

"Then say your name," Dray said.

Miko opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She had coast tickets under three bought names, but none of them were hers anymore. She had burned the last two. She had nothing.

"Scale doesn't care," Dray said. "Step on."

She stepped on. The dial spun and stopped at a number—one-twenty-seven, maybe, though she wasn't looking at the numbers so much as the man writing them down in a ledger bolted to the scale housing. Dray didn't introduce himself as the writer. He just wrote.

"One-twenty-seven," Dray said. "Short rate. You draw water at the short rate until you're read out at the plate. Second bell, you're either on a plate or on the shelf with the sleepers. Understand?"

Miko looked past him at the shed. The roll door was climbing, slow and groaning, and behind it rose eleven dark shapes. Off-board rigs. Transponders pulled. No board to answer to. They sat in the dark. They did not move.

"And if I don't want either?" Miko asked.

Dray looked at her, expressionless. "Then you stay on the scale until someone names you. The yard doesn't run on wants."

Miko shifted her weight. The iron was cold through her boots. "What happens to the sleepers?"

"They sleep until a plate dies," Dray said. "Then they go on the pile. You want to be a pile?"

"No."

"Then find a name before the second bell." He pointed at the shed. The door kept climbing. Eleven rigs. Forty riders, he had said. Forty plates wired shut to sternums. And one name missing from her own chest.

Miko spat into the dirt. "I had a name once. Culvert Nine's station loader. Badge C9-047."

"Then you should have kept it," Dray said. He turned and walked toward the shed, his boots heavy on the gravel. "Second bell rings when that door hits the top."

Miko stood on the scale. The dial still read one-twenty-seven. Ahead, the eleventh dark shape rose into the light, silent and blank, waiting for someone to say its name.

Miko stepped off the scale. The iron left a cold ring in her soles. She walked after Dray into the shed.

The roll door groaned all the way up, and light came in under it in sheets. Eleven rigs stood in two rows, hoods cold, transponder sockets empty where the little black boxes had been wrenched out. A transponder answers a reader; without one, the rig doesn't exist on any node's board. These rigs had no board to answer to.

Dray walked beside her, boots loud on the concrete. "Forty riders," he said. "Forty plates."

Miko looked at the line of bodies slumped between the rigs. Each rider sat with their back against a tire or a bulkhead, head lolling, a steel crew plate wired shut over the sternum. The plate carried the rig's living name. A name wired to steel kept the engine authorized, kept the fuel pump cycling, kept the rig alive. A blank plate meant a parts pile, and a parts pile meant no rider.

"Forty names," Miko said. "And I don't have one."

"Find one," Dray said.

They reached the last row. One rider sat slumped forward, chest rising slow. The wire around his plate hung loose, one strand snapped, the steel tag tilted against his ribs. The plate was blank, or the name had been worn off. Miko could see the rider's throat move under the wire. He was breathing.

"That one's not sleeping," Miko said.

"No," Dray said. "He's waiting for someone to cut the wire properly and say the name that goes under it. Until then, his rig won't turn over. And he won't walk out."

Miko looked at the cut wire. "Who cut it?"

"Someone who didn't want to wait for the second bell," Dray said. He pointed at a rig behind the man, hood cold, transponder socket empty. "That rig sleeps with him. No name, no power. That's the rule."

Miko stepped closer to the rider. His eyes were open, flat and gray, tracking her without moving his head. She had no badge. No name. Three coast tickets burned to ash. And here was a man who knew exactly what it cost to be unwired.

"You said forty," Miko said. "I count forty."

"Good count," Dray said. "Now decide which one you're going to be. Because the second bell doesn't care about your math."

A bell rang somewhere in the yard, low and once. Not the second. A warning.

Miko looked at the cut wire again, then at the eleven blank rigs. "If I say a name, whose rig does it wake?"

Dray didn't answer. He walked back toward the door plate, his shadow stretching long across the concrete, and left her standing between a breathing man and a rig that wouldn't start.

Miko walked the row with her hands in her pockets, counting plates. Each rider had a steel tag the size of a playing card wired at the sternum, three strands of baling wire twisted off at the side. The names were stamped, not written. She was looking for a gap between the tags and there wasn't one. Forty riders, forty plates, all of them somebody's.

Halfway down the second row a boy lifted his head as she passed. Seventeen, maybe. Shaved at the temples, sunburned across the nose in the shape of a collar. His plate sat crooked, the wire pulled tight enough to pucker his shirt.

"You're the new one-twenty-seven," he said.

"Dray tell you?"

"Dray writes it in the book and the book's on the scale housing. Everybody reads the book." He tipped his chin at her, friendly as a man selling water. "Corwin Adley. That's a good one. Kettering side, died in a stairwell two winters back, nobody's going to check a stairwell."

Miko stopped walking. "You're giving me a name."

"I don't sell. Selling's for Brill." He shrugged, and the wire at his chest took the shrug and held it. "Free. Take it to the end bench before the bell and Sorge will cut you a plate."

"Why would you do that?"

"You looked like you needed one." He said it like the answer was obvious, and maybe to him it was. "Petra Sill, if Adley's too rich for you. Seal clerk out of Bay Four, retired, bad hip, nobody's called on her in a year. Two for two. I've got a whole drawer of them."

Boots on concrete. Dray had come back up the row with a can of water in one hand, and he stopped beside them without any hurry at all.

"He gives a name to anyone who asks," Dray said. "Ask him twice, he'll give you two. That's why there's nothing of his in my book and nothing of his on my board."

"Because every name he hands out burns the next one," Miko said.

"Because nobody can write down a boy who won't hold still for it." Dray looked at Tobin the way a man looks at a gauge he's already read. "He's been seventeen for three years."

"I'm seventeen," Tobin said.

"Nineteen, then."

"Seventeen." The boy grinned, and it was a real grin, and it didn't reach anywhere near his eyes. "You want the truth, one-twenty-seven? A board's a list. A list's an address. You put a name on a board and inside a week somebody with a claim comes down the line reading it out loud, and then you're cargo with a number on it." He nodded at her coat. "You know. You were on one."

"Two hours ago," Miko said. "Steel, in ink, my own hand. Station loader, Culvert Nine."

"And?"

"And a man with a book told Brill to rub it off, and she rubbed it off, because she can't say no to a trade." Miko's mouth had gone dry enough that swallowing hurt. "Now I'm a number Dray wrote down."

"So you know what I'm saving you from." Tobin leaned his head back against the tire behind him. "Adley's better than the scale. Take Adley."

"And be nobody for the rest of my life."

"You're nobody now. I'm offering you a *comfortable* nobody. There's a bunk in rig nine with your number on it and the water's the same either way."

Dray set the can down on the concrete between them, and Miko heard the short-rate measure of it, half a cup, no more until the plate. He walked on toward the door, and the rope for the second bell swung a little where it hung by the roll door, moving in the wind coming under the steel.

Tobin's grin went out. He looked at her collar, at the empty loop of wire where the badge had hung, and when he spoke again it was low, under the sound of the door.

"Are you carrying a name you can spare?"

Miko shook her head.

"No," she said.

Tobin pushed off the tire and started walking. "Then you're staying on the scale until someone decides you're worth a plate. Come on."

The end bench sat under the shed's far window, a concrete slab with a vise bolted to it. Amil Sorge stood behind it, thin and bald, wearing an apron scored with old cuts. Their crew plate was blank steel wired to their sternum—no name, just the smooth rectangle where one had been. A seal knife lay beside a coil of fresh wire.

"Name first," Amil said. "Then the cut. Two witnesses, or it doesn't count."

Tobin looked at Miko. "You got a name?"

Miko thought of J. Renner, dead on Anza's board. She thought of Corwin Adley, a stairwell death Tobin pulled from thin air. She thought of Miko Keres, rubbed off Culvert Nine's steel by Brill's own hand. None of them were hers to give.

"I don't have one," Miko said.

"Then borrow one," Tobin said. He turned to Amil. "Corwin Adley. Say it again so it sticks."

Amil lifted the seal knife. Miko and Tobin stood on either side of the bench. Amil nodded at a rider slumped against the far bulkhead, a plate wired shut over his sternum. "That plate already wears a name. Corwin Adley isn't on it."

"So?" Tobin said.

"So I cut the name spoken. I don't invent plates." Amil tapped the knife against their palm. "Two witnesses. You both heard it."

Amil turned to a blank plate lying in the vise. They slipped the knife under the wire twist and cut. One strand snapped. Then the second. The wire fell away. The plate clattered to the concrete, blank side up.

Amil's own plate shivered. A single stamped letter lifted off the steel like ash in a draft and was gone. Amil touched their sternum, fingers tracing the empty space.

"One fewer," Amil said. Their voice was flat. "You say it, I cut it, I lose it. That's the rule."

Miko stared at Amil's chest. The plate was blank again. She didn't ask what had lifted off it. She looked at Tobin.

Tobin's grin was gone. "Corwin Adley's not mine," he said quietly. "It's just a name I keep in my pocket."

"You said it aloud," Amil said. "Before two witnesses. The cut is done. Now who are you, one-twenty-seven? Say your name and I'll wire you to a plate before the second bell."

Miko opened her mouth. She had coast tickets under bought names, ash in the stove at Culvert Nine, and a badge that belonged to a dead manifest. She had nothing.

The wind came under the roll door, cold and sudden. Amil's hand rested on the seal knife. The blade caught the light.

Miko's throat worked. The first word that formed wasn't a lie. It was her own.

"Miko—"

Dray's voice came from the door plate, not the end bench. He had crossed the shed while she stood with her mouth open, and now he stood between her and Amil, blocking the seal knife.

"Leave it," he said. "Come look at the page."

Amil's fingers stayed on the knife's wrapped handle, but they didn't lift it. Miko stepped off the concrete bench. Her boots rang on the floor. Dray led her past the sleeping riders, past the man with the cut wire still breathing slow against his tire, to a steel desk bolted under the shed's far window. A working page lay open there, grease-stained and dog-eared. Dray slapped a palm over it.

"Don't look yet," he said.

She didn't. He uncovered it when she was close enough to smell the ink.

Culvert Nine's count sat at the top: eleven, struck full in steel. Beneath it, Brill's name ranked above a list of names—her crew, Miko saw, each one indented like a debt coming due. Bricks of salt. Cans of fuel. A calendar written in notches.

"You see that?" Dray said. "Eleven cans. Eleven names she owes and won't hand over without a trade. She can't refuse a trade either. The whole ore line knows it."

He turned the page. A clean sheet. He tapped it once, hard.

"My book," he said. "Plate 4217. Rig Seven from my own count. Dark eleven months. Culvert Nine's reader logged eleven cans against it, and I know that plate on sight." He looked at Miko, expressionless. "I'll read it at the door plate the day someone brings me a living name and two witnesses. Not before."

Miko stared at the blank page. "You're going back down the line."

"To buy her crew one can at a time. A can for a name. She pays me in names, I pay her in cans, and the rigs roll with plates wired tight. That's the plan."

"And if nobody gives you a name?"

Dray's fingers stayed on the page. "Then the book stays closed. The rigs stay dark. And you stay one-twenty-seven on my scale until the second bell rings."

He lifted his hand. The empty page waited. The wind came under the roll door, cold and sudden. Miko understood she was the only person in the shed who had just watched a name get cut and still had one of her own left to spend.

Dray capped the ink and shut the working page under his arm. "One can, one name," he said. "I roll back down before the light's gone."

Miko had stopped listening to the plan. She was back at the end bench in her head—the seal knife, the blank plate, the single stamped letter that had lifted off Amil's chest like ash in a draft. A living name, said out loud, with two people near enough to hear it. That was the whole lever. Not a badge on a coat loop. Not ink a woman could rub off with her thumb. Not one of Tobin's stairwell dead. A name still *on* somebody, spoken in front of witnesses, and the knife did the rest.

She had one of those. Had it the whole time, walking around under Dray's chalked number like a coin sewn into a hem.

"You're going back down the line," she said. "Leaving me on the scale."

"Second bell hasn't rung." Dray lifted the hand lamp off the desk—brass, shuttered, throwing a hard white circle and nothing past it. "Door hits the top, you're on a plate or on the shelf. Same clock everybody in here started on."

"And if I had a name to spend?"

He looked at her the way he'd read the scale dial. A number, not a person. "Then you spend it before the bell, not after. Not my business. My business is cans." He turned for the roll door, and the white circle swung with him, over the sleepers, over the man with the cut wire still breathing against his tire, over forty wired chests. "Watch the door. Learn the count. I come back up with Brill's people behind me, you'll see how a name buys a rig."

He walked. The circle went with him and the shed sank back into the gray under the window.

Miko stood one more second with her own name still in her mouth. Two witnesses. The bench was thirty feet off. The rope by the roll door hung dead still. She could be wired to steel before it ever swung—

The lamp stopped.

Dray had halted at the threshold, the white circle pinned on the dirt just past the door plate. Down the spur, out of the dark, a second light had come up. Not a lamp on a pole. A headlight—high, square, growing—throwing the door plate's shadow long across the ground toward the open shed. Aimed at the door. At the sleepers. At the two of them standing in it.

Dray didn't step off his own concrete to meet it. He held the lamp steady and watched the light swell.

"Company," he said, flat as a gauge needle. "And nobody's written on my book for tonight."

The headlight filled the door.
